newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia sees Serbian opposition as threat to peace.
newsitem.headline: Croatia sees Serbian opposition as threat to peace.

text.p: Embattled President Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia won unexpected political support on Friday when former war enemy Croatia said the Serbian opposition movement could be a threat to peace if it gained power.

"Croatia has no interest in favouring Milosevic...but at this moment the Serbian opposition does not offer any guarantees for maintaining the peace," said Zlatko Canjuga, a political adviser to President Franjo Tudjman.
Croatia won a devastating war for independence from Serbian-led Yugoslavia in 1991 and in 1995 recaptured parts of its territory held by Milosevic-backed Serb rebels.
But Yugoslavia and Croatia established diplomatic relations late last year after a surprise Milosevic-Tudjman summit.

In an interview for the Friday issue of the daily Slobodna Dalmacija, Canjuga warned the international community about what he called dangerous nationalist rhetoric by leading figures in Serbia's opposition movement.

He was referring to Vuk Draskovic and Zoran Djindjic, co-leaders of mass street protests in Belgrade in the past eight weeks against Milosevic's refusal to confirm the opposition's victory in municipal elections last November.
The movement, seen elsewhere largely as a call for more political freedom in socialist-dominated Serbia, is regarded with suspicion in Croatia for its rightist element.
"The international community needs to be very careful about Draskovic and Djindjic, regarding the statements they made during the (1991) war," Canjuga said.

Both Draskovic and Djindjic supported Yugoslav army intervention in Croatia and criticised Milosevic for withdrawing his support from warring Bosnian Serbs in 1994 to win a lifting of United Nations sanctions.
Several recent editorials in leading Croatian state media recalled anti-Croatian statements by Djindjic and Draskovic in 1991 and their ties with Bosnian Serbs and the Yugoslav army.

Television pictures of Serbian demonstrators today carrying nationalist flags and insignia and raising three fingers remind many Croats of similar crowds in the late 1980s who backed Milosevic and his moves that led to wars in Croatia and Bosnia.
"Milosevic is that real factor with which the international community negotiated the peace (in Bosnia and Croatia), and he should be treated as such," Canjuga said.
"Croatia's position has to be (for) peace ... That is our main interest," he added.
Canjuga questioned the readiness of the Serbian opposition to accept and respect commitments made by Milosevic leading to the U.S.-sponsored Dayton peace treaty on Bosnia in 1995.
"Statements of some opposition leaders have been aimed at throwing a spotlight on some old Serbian pretensions towards parts of Croatian territory," he said.

Croats regard Milosevic as the person most responsible for the 1990s nationalist wars in old Yugoslavia, masterminding the Yugoslav army attempt to carve up parts of Croatia and Bosnia with the help of their substantial Serb minorities.

But since 1991 Milosevic has strengthened his police at the expense of the army and sacrified some Bosnian Serb territorial goals in exchange for peace, securing himself the status of "the devil we know" in the eyes of Croats and Bosnian Moslems.
These moves, and the Dayton agreement, put Milosevic into the role of preferred partner for the Croatian government, now in deep crisis because Tudjman is seriously ill.
The 74-year-old Croatian leader has matched wits with Milosevic for years, steering Croatia to a victorious war in 1991 and the reconquest of Serb-held enclaves in 1995.
Independent Croatian analysts shared Canjuga's view.
"I find their position logical," said Zarko Puhovski, an analyst normally critical of Croatia's nationalist government.
"Democratisation of Serbia and Croatia would put the peace in Bosnia in greater jeopardy than it is now," he said.
